column2: At first the ship pushed through. Then the ice got thicker.
On the nineteenth of January 1915, a day's sail from land, the ice closed around Endurance. It was stuck.
The crew went out with picks, saws and chisels and tried to cut a channel. It did not move an inch.
And now the ice itself began to drift. Taking the ship with it, away from the coast where they had planned to land.
Then winter came. In Antarctica that means months without the sun.
They lived on board. They played football on the ice, held dog races, and kept each other going.
The ship's photographer, Frank Hurley, took pictures of everything.
But the ice was not still. It was pressing in from both sides, and the wooden hull began to groan.
On the twenty-fourth of October 1915, the ice broke through. Water poured into the ship.
For three days the men pumped, in turns, around the clock. The water rose faster than they could pump it out.
On the twenty-seventh of October, Shackleton gave the order. Abandon ship.
They had been trapped for nine months. Now they were camped on floating ice, with no radio, no way to call for help, and nobody in the world who knew where they were.
